docs.title: Tool, Project Origin, and Extent
docs.text:
OpenAI Codex assisted with the existing solo sports statistics project and coursework. The exact underlying model identifier was not exposed in this session. The student may add the model name shown in the application interface if available; an unverified model name should not be invented.

The sports topic was already present in the repository and conversation before this midterm preparation. AI helped refine the experiment and substantially implement and document the milestone. Assistance went beyond proofreading: it included Python source, tests, cloud-command integration, source research, data conversion, execution of local checks, interpretation, report drafting, and presentation materials. No unsupported percentage of AI-written work is claimed.

docs.title: Helpful Results
docs.text: AI assistance connected implementation to specific course requirements, kept synthetic and real data separate, and produced executable checks. The experiment also retained an unfavorable result: logistic regression did not beat the constant 50% forecast on the selected 72 games. AI-generated explanations were checked against the actual JSON output.

docs.title: Failures and Limits
docs.text:
• Earlier screenshot attachments were unavailable in some exchanges. A missing image could not establish that a command worked. Only accessible originals and observed outputs are cited as evidence.
  • Older documents contained stale test counts and unfinished recovery checks. The report now separates October 1 Mac evidence from October 15 preparation-environment results.
  • The earlier upstream PR was too broad and had conflicts. Its closed, unmerged status is stated; the successor is limited to one Google issue.
  • A Google driver fallback looked usable but did not instantiate Libcloud's actual GCE driver. Focused tests now check the real constructor contract.
  • GitHub writes were denied by permissions. A prepared patch is not a published contribution. Cloud plans and mocked tests do not establish live cloud operation.
  • Passing software tests do not imply good forecasts. The constant baseline has the lowest measured error.

docs.title: Responsibility and In-Class Explanation
docs.text:
Before presenting, the student must review the changes, run the local commands, and be able to explain the dataset license, strict threshold event, chronological split, Brier score, baseline result, and each cloud's status. Student review and independent understanding have not been verified by this AI session. The assistance must be acknowledged when discussing code and documents rather than presenting the generated material as wholly unaided work.

The application does not call an LLM service. Development assistance and the statistical classifier are distinct uses of AI. Paid-service costs and open alternatives are described in the cost appendix.

Sources: Piazza #111, #88, #100, and #101.

docs.title: SPORTSSTATS: AWS Setup
docs.text: AWS is the selected public cloud. On October 15, the student connected to the running EC2 instance, transferred the source, passed all 34 application tests, ran the historical model, and opened the dashboard through an SSH tunnel. The visible results are recorded in AWS evidence. Full cmx automation remains unfinished. The project still needs Multipass and an OpenStack cloud as well.

docs.title: 1. Import the Existing Public Key
docs.text:
The Mac key was created at ~/.ssh/sports_midterm_aws. Changing the project name does not rename that file. Import only its .pub public file into AWS.

In Mac Terminal, run:

pbcopy < ~/.ssh/sports_midterm_aws.pub

In the Ohio-region EC2 → Key pairs → Import key pair page, set Name to sports-midterm-aws. Clear Public key contents, then press Command-V. The pasted text should begin ssh-ed25519. The pbcopy command itself does not belong in that box. Click Import key pair, then select it in the instance launch page.

The instructor requires passphrases and ssh-agent/Keychain. The 10:43 am Mac screenshot showed a passphrase prompt followed by Identity added after ssh-add --apple-use-keychain, confirming that this AWS key was unlocked and loaded into the agent. The instructor's full cmx key scan and cmx key github list outputs still need to be shown separately. Keep the private file and passphrase off GitHub and out of screenshots.

docs.title: 2. Launch Settings
docs.text:
Setting Value Region Ohio, us-east-2 Name tag SPORTSSTATS Image Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS Architecture 64-bit x86 Instance type t3.micro Key pair sports-midterm-aws SSH source My IP HTTP/HTTPS Leave unchecked for the first test Storage 8 GiB Instance count 1

The earlier screenshot showed Ubuntu 26.04; select 24.04 to match the project setup. Check the account's Free-plan credit balance before launching. Current costs and limits are in the appendix.

docs.title: 3. Connect and Run the Application
docs.text:
After launch, wait for Running and passing status checks. Use the instance's Connect → SSH client page to get its actual public address. Ubuntu uses the username ubuntu; the Mac private-key path remains ~/.ssh/sports_midterm_aws. Confirm the host fingerprint through EC2 before accepting an unfamiliar host key.

Transfer tracked project source without data or credentials. A source-only archive can be made in the Mac repository with git archive; download the pinned historical dataset inside the guest. Keep the remote project at ~/sports-project to match the cmx smoke command.

In the guest, from that project directory, the application checks are:

python3 --version
make -C sports test
make -C sports history
make -C sports model

Python 3.12+ is required. Skip history after a successful import. Expected data counts are 2,460 team-game rows, 1,230 games, and 30 teams. The Chicago comparison uses 72 games and reports logistic Brier about 0.2533 versus constant 0.2500. Save genuine command output with its environment and time; do not publish key details.

For the first dashboard test, bind the guest server to 127.0.0.1 and use an SSH tunnel from the Mac. This avoids opening dashboard port 8000 to the Internet. This configuration was observed working at 2:28 pm, using Mac port 8001 and guest port 8000. Keep both Terminal sessions open while using the foreground server. The full database totals, lower model comparison, persistent service, and live cmx integration still need direct verification.

docs.title: 4. cmx Requirement
docs.text:
python3 -m sports.cloud plan --cloud aws prints the commands for SPORTSSTATS. It does not run them. Do not run the printed start command against a VM already created in the console. The audited upstream AWS provider has unresolved driver/method issues. A successful console deployment would prove the app runs on EC2; live cmx integration remains a separate requirement.

After the provider, source, and data are working, this checks the guest model through cmx:

python3 -m sports.cloud smoke --cloud aws --name SPORTSSTATS

Do not mark it complete without a real successful result. Keep any AWS provider fix separate from the prepared Google-only contribution and open only one upstream PR at a time.

Sources: EC2 key-pair import, launch wizard, AWS Free Tier, and Week 7.

Acknowledgment: OpenAI Codex drafted this guide. Selected settings and observed account status are distinguished from unverified deployment steps.

docs.title: Prepared Google Candidate
docs.text:
Title: Google: initialize the actual Libcloud GCE driver

Problem: The provider imports a nonexistent driver path and falls back to a dummy class, while its supplied keyword arguments do not match the actual GCE constructor. This prevents a meaningful Google connection.

Change: Import GCENodeDriver from libcloud.compute.drivers.gce, pass service account, key, project and zone using supported argument names, and raise ConfigError before authentication when required fields are missing.

Scope: Four files, 63 additions and 18 deletions: src/cloudmesh/ai/vm/google/GoogleManager.py and tests/unit/test_google_driver_initialization.py, plus Google fixture/assertion updates in tests/unit/test_hyperscalers.py and tests/unit/test_libcloud_providers.py. No shared CLI, other provider, hostlist, existing test rewrite, or documentation change is included.

Validation: Seven Google-focused tests pass, including four new constructor checks. They use an autospecced real driver constructor and cover missing configuration. They do not create resources or prove the rest of the Google lifecycle works. The sports suite is not a substitute for provider validation. A broader 22-test run reports 21 passes and one AWS unsupported-method failure; that exact failure also reproduces on unmodified dev2. It stays outside this Google-only change.

Publication status: Prepared locally, not submitted. Before opening a PR, update from dev2, inspect its current driver/tests, and rerun the focused test. If upstream already contains the fix, do not submit duplicate work. The old PR remains closed.

docs.title: Prepared Key-Scanner Candidate
docs.text:
Title: Key scan: check passphrases without prompting

Problem: In a real Terminal, the scanner's ssh-keygen -y -f command can prompt for an encrypted key's passphrase. After the user unlocks it, the command succeeds and the scanner incorrectly labels the key as unprotected. This happened during the October 15 Mac check.

Change: Add -P "" to the existing probe. The probe explicitly tries an empty passphrase and does not ask the user to unlock the key.

Scope: Two files, 81 additions and one deletion: one changed command in src/cloudmesh/ai/vm/key_manager.py, plus tests/unit/test_key_passphrase.py. Existing tests are preserved. Provider code, key filename discovery, documentation, and SPORTSSTATS code are outside this patch.

Validation: Two tests create temporary real Ed25519 keys. They check an unprotected key and an encrypted key in a terminal. The encrypted-key regression test fails against unchanged dev2 because a prompt appears. Both pass with the fix. No account key or passphrase is used by these tests.

Publication status: Isolated branch based on dev2 f55d7bd, not published or applied to the student's installed instructor code. This candidate is held for student review. It must not be combined with the Google change in one PR. The student's real GitHub key-list check also needs the GitHub CLI and account authentication; this scanner fix does not complete that separate check.

docs.title: Appendix: SPORTSSTATS Costs and Open Alternatives
docs.text:
Checked October 15, 2026. The account screen and launch price are observations from that morning. The worked estimate is not an actual bill.

Component Current use or estimate Free/open alternative Application Python standard library, SQLite, HTML/JS; no paid application API Run the same code locally Historical data FiveThirtyEight NBA data, CC BY 4.0; no purchase Separate synthetic fixture for software checks Multipass Local CPU, RAM, disk, electricity; no provider VM bill Direct host execution; Multipass is open source Chameleon KVM@TACC Needs an approved allocation and quota; access unverified Local Multipass; remote portability still needs testing Amazon EC2 Selected public cloud; t3.micro in Ohio, Ubuntu 24.04, 8 GiB disk Local Multipass or an eligible Chameleon allocation ## AWS Account and Worked Estimate

The student's AWS account screen showed Free plan, $100 credits remaining, 183 days remaining, with April 15, 2027 shown as the end date. This was observed on October 15 at about 8:48 am Chicago time. AWS states that its Free plan ends after six months or when credits run out, whichever happens first. The balance and terms must be checked again before use. No paid-plan upgrade was performed during this preparation.

The Ohio (us-east-2) launch screen displayed a Linux t3.micro compute rate of $0.0104/hour. A 15-minute run at that rate is $0.0026 in compute: 0.25 × 0.0104. This is a planning calculation before applying credits. It excludes EBS storage, public IPv4, data transfer, possible surplus CPU credits, taxes, and other resources. The selected instance has 2 virtual CPUs and 1 GiB RAM. The application later passed 34 guest tests and displayed the historical NBA dashboard on this instance.

A running EC2 instance, SSH access, guest tests, and the deployed dashboard were confirmed in the afternoon screenshots. Actual charges and the current credit balance have not been checked. Google Cloud was considered earlier but is no longer the selected public cloud. Neither Google AI Pro nor a paid sports-data service is needed for this application.

docs.title: Cost Controls
docs.text:
Use one small instance and a short test. Check the Free-plan balance and available usage alerts. A budget alert alone does not stop spending. Stopping a VM can leave storage and other billable resources behind. After preserving the needed results, remove the dedicated VM and unneeded disks or addresses, then check inventory and billing. Keep the account on its Free plan unless a separate decision is made to upgrade.

The course guidelines require billing alarms on commercial cloud accounts. No configured AWS billing alarm has been observed yet; Free-plan credits do not complete that requirement. On OpenStack, use Chameleon KVM@TACC and the smallest suitable VM. Shelve or delete it when idle; stopping alone is not sufficient under the assignment's resource rule.

docs.title: Why These Services
docs.text: The model is a small CPU-only classifier. It needs no GPU or hosted LLM. Local Python and SQLite keep the analysis reproducible without a subscription. The remote clouds are used to test deployment and repeat the same calculation, not to change the model's accuracy.

docs.title: SPORTSSTATS on an Existing Ubuntu VM
docs.text: This installs the same historical NBA application on an existing Ubuntu 24.04 guest. It changes only the student's application and a new sportsstats.service; it does not edit cmx, launch a VM, or stop the working port-8000 dashboard. It is prepared and locally checked, not yet verified on a live guest.

docs.title: Review and Package
docs.text:
Review sports/install-guest.sh before running it. The guest must use the account ubuntu or cc, with non-interactive sudo. Python 3.12+ and SQLite support are required. The source belongs in ~/sports-project.

After reviewing and committing the installer in the student's course repository, make a source-only archive on the Mac:

git archive --format=tar.gz --output=/tmp/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz HEAD sports

The archive uses committed source. Raw data and keys are excluded. Existing databases are not replaced by this installer.

docs.title: Multipass
docs.text:
First check multipass list. These commands target the existing project VM sports-midterm; use them only if that VM is present and running.

multipass transfer /tmp/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz sports-midterm:/home/ubuntu/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz
multipass exec sports-midterm -- bash -lc 'mkdir -p ~/sports-project && tar -xzf ~/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz -C ~/sports-project && bash ~/sports-project/sports/install-guest.sh'

docs.title: AWS or Chameleon
docs.text:
Use the actual guest address, key, and username from the existing VM. AWS Ubuntu uses ubuntu; the earlier Chameleon image used cc. The example placeholders below must be replaced with those values. Keep private key contents on the Mac.

scp -i KEY_PATH /tmp/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz GUEST_USER@GUEST_ADDRESS:SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz
ssh -i KEY_PATH -o ServerAliveInterval=30 GUEST_USER@GUEST_ADDRESS 'mkdir -p ~/sports-project && tar -xzf ~/SPORTSSTATS-source.tar.gz -C ~/sports-project && bash ~/sports-project/sports/install-guest.sh'

The installer runs the application tests, imports the pinned historical dataset if missing, and enables a systemd service. It then checks the real HTTP health and model output. Expected output includes 2,460 rows, 72 evaluated Chicago games, logistic Brier 0.2533129305645343, and constant Brier 0.25. Save actual output for each guest; a prepared command is not a live result.

docs.title: View the Separate Service
docs.text:
The service binds to guest 127.0.0.1:8765. To view a remote SSH guest from the Mac, open another Terminal tab with a distinct unused local port:

ssh -i KEY_PATH -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -N -L 127.0.0.1:8002:127.0.0.1:8765 GUEST_USER@GUEST_ADDRESS

Open http://127.0.0.1:8002 and keep that tunnel tab open. Use a different local port for another guest. Do not replace the existing AWS port-8001 tunnel until the new service has been verified. A Multipass guest can also be checked with multipass exec sports-midterm -- curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/health.

For a failed install, inspect the guest's systemctl status sportsstats.service and journalctl -u sportsstats.service --no-pager -n 40. A successful install does not establish VM provisioning through cmx or complete the instructor's three-cloud requirement. Those results must be checked separately.

Acknowledgment: OpenAI Codex wrote this installer and guide. Live guest installation and student review are still needed.

docs.title: SPORTSSTATS Presentation Notes
docs.text: Open root project.md for the instructor's review. The slides are optional. This suggested five-to-seven-minute pace is for practice; it is not an instructor-set time limit. Spoken notes can use first person; the report stays in third person.

docs.title: Opening
docs.text: “My project is called SPORTSSTATS. It looks at basketball scores and how often a team passes a points target. It has a terminal command, an API, and a dashboard. The current version adds real NBA team data and a small machine-learning model.”

docs.title: Data
docs.text: “The data comes from FiveThirtyEight and has a CC BY 4.0 license. The import uses the 2014–15 NBA regular season. There are 1,230 games and 30 teams. Each game has a row for each team, so there are 2,460 rows. These are team scores, not real player statistics. The older player demo uses made-up data.”

docs.title: Model and Live Demo
docs.text:
“The question is whether Chicago scores more than 100.5 points. The model uses the previous game and the average of the five games before it. It makes each prediction before seeing that day's result. All three methods are compared on the same 72 games.”

Run these from the repository root only after the historical import has succeeded:

python3 -m sports --db sports/data/history.sqlite3 model --team CHI --threshold 100.5
make -C sports historical-serve

For a local server, open http://127.0.0.1:8000. The working AWS dashboard uses the existing Mac SSH tunnel at http://127.0.0.1:8001. Keep both AWS Terminal tabs open. Keep CHI, Team total, All opponents, and threshold 100.5. Show the 82-game history, then the separate 72-game machine-learning comparison. If the live demo fails, label the aggregate JSON as saved evidence.

“Chicago passed the target in 43 of 82 games, about 52%. The model's Brier score is 0.2533. The simple 50% forecast scores 0.2500. A lower score is better, so the model did not beat that simple forecast. One team and one season are not enough to claim it predicts future games well.”

Brier means the average squared gap between a probability and the actual result, recorded as zero or one. Always predicting 0.5 gives 0.25 for every outcome. The older historical-only panel starts scoring after five games; use the separate model panel for the fair three-method comparison.

Only replace these pending statements with results actually observed before the talk.

docs.text: "The remaining items are the full live model comparison, complete key checks, reviewed publication, updated local and Chameleon results, cmx automation, and confirmation of project and cloud approval. The next model check should use more seasons and teams with settings chosen before looking at results. Live NBA data will come later."

docs.title: Questions to Practice
docs.text:
Question Plain answer Why this model? It is a small classifier for a yes/no event and runs on CPU. It can be compared with simple forecasts. Why 82 games versus 72? The history uses all games. The evaluation skips ten games to build prior history. How is future information kept out? Inputs use earlier games. Each day's predictions happen before that day's results update the model. What does the interval mean? It shows uncertainty in the historical rate under assumptions. It does not guarantee the next game's outcome. Are there real player stats? No. The real data is team totals; the player demo is synthetic. Is the contribution merged? No. The old PR is closed; the smaller fix is prepared locally. Did AI do all the work? State the actual assistance. Do not claim the generated changes were written without AI.

Before the talk, read sports/history.py, sports/model.py, sports/cloud.py, and their tests. Practice explaining one prediction and its later update. Correct any statement that is not supported by the actual results.

Acknowledgment: OpenAI Codex drafted these notes in simpler words. They still need student review and practice.

docs.title: SPORTSSTATS
docs.text:
• Sydel Ugwu
  • COMP 388
  • Midterm progress report
  • October 15, 2026

Cloud choices: Multipass, Jetstream2 (OpenStack), and Amazon (AWS).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
SPORTSSTATS is Sydel Ugwu's solo project for exploring basketball scores and comparing predictions. Users can choose a team and a points target, then see how often that team passed the target. The project uses Python and SQLite, with a terminal interface, a JSON API, and a web dashboard.

The current version uses real NBA team scores from the 2014–15 regular season. It also includes a small logistic regression model that learns from earlier games. For Chicago, the model did slightly better than a forecast based on the team's past results, but a simple 50% forecast had the lowest error. That result is part of the project, even though the model did not come out ahead.

On October 15, the application passed 34 tests on the Mac and 34 tests on an Ubuntu AWS instance. The historical dashboard also opened from AWS through an SSH tunnel. The sections below explain those results, the three cloud choices, and the evidence still needed for the full cloud setup.

docs.title: Project Goal and Research Question
docs.text:
The goal is to make basketball statistics easier to explore and check whether a small model can improve on simple predictions. An average score gives some information, but it does not show how often a team passed a particular target.

Research question: For Chicago's 2014–15 regular season, does a logistic regression model using earlier games predict scoring above 100.5 points more accurately than a historical-rate forecast or a constant 50% forecast?

The current project covers team scores, data import, probability estimates, model comparisons, and the dashboard. The earlier demo uses fictional player records to test player and opponent filters. The real dataset contains team totals. Real player data, more seasons, and live NBA data are planned for later. The project does not offer guaranteed predictions or real-money betting.

docs.title: Data and Application Design
docs.text:
The historical data comes from FiveThirtyEight and is available under CC BY 4.0. The selected season has 1,230 games and 30 teams. Each game has a row for each team, giving 2,460 team-game rows. FiveThirtyEight credits Basketball-Reference for the original game information.

The importer downloads a fixed source version and checks its SHA-256 checksum before using it. This helps keep repeated runs on the same data. SQLite checks for duplicate records and inconsistent scores. Replacing an existing dataset requires an explicit option. Raw downloads, databases, VM disks, and credentials stay out of Git.

flowchart TD
    D["NBA / demo data"] --> S["SQLite checks"]
    S --> A["Stats / model"]
    A --> C["CLI / JSON API"]
    C --> W["Dashboard"]
    V["VM / cmx"] --> C

The terminal and dashboard use the same analysis code. The dashboard gives users a way to explore the results visually, while the CLI and API allow the same analysis to run without it.

docs.title: AI Model and Evaluation
docs.text:
The model predicts whether Chicago scores strictly more than 100.5 points. It uses the previous game's score and the average score from the five earlier games. Both inputs are measured relative to the target and divided by 20. The model also includes an intercept.

Weights start at zero, and the learning rate is 0.05. Training begins after five earlier games. Scoring begins after ten earlier games, leaving 72 games for comparison. The model predicts each date's games before learning from that date's results. This prevents a game's outcome, or another outcome from the same date, from entering its prediction.

All three forecasts use the same 72 evaluation games. The historical forecast uses earlier results with smoothing, while the constant forecast always predicts 50%. The settings were fixed before this reported experiment. This is an early check on one team and one season, rather than a broad test of NBA prediction accuracy.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Chicago 2014–15 regular season Result Games in the historical summary 82 Games above 100.5 points 43 Average team points 100.79 Historical rate above the target 52.44% 95% Wilson interval for that rate 41.76%–62.90% Games used to compare all three forecasts 72 Logistic model Brier score 0.2533 Historical-rate Brier score 0.2572 Constant 50% Brier score 0.2500

Brier score measures the average squared difference between a predicted probability and the result, recorded as zero or one. A lower score is better. Always predicting 50% gives a score of 0.2500, which beat the model's 0.2533 in this experiment.

The model's small improvement over the historical forecast does not show that it will work better on other teams or seasons. The Wilson interval describes uncertainty in the historical rate under an independent-game assumption. Games within a season can influence one another, which limits that interpretation. The interval does not guarantee what will happen in the next game.

The dashboard also has an older historical-only comparison that skips five games and scores 77. The separate model panel uses the correct shared group of 72 games for the three-way comparison.

docs.text:
Make targets group the common test, import, model, and server commands. Automated tests check data handling, model timing, and agreement between the CLI and API. Git commits keep the data, model, interface, cloud, and documentation work in smaller pieces.

The existing Multipass deployment script creates a dedicated Ubuntu 24.04 VM, transfers source, runs tests, and sets up a systemd service. The database stays on the guest disk. The earlier service restart was checked on October 1.

An installer for existing Ubuntu VMs is also prepared. It runs tests, imports missing historical data, and creates a separate service on guest port 8765. Shell and service-file checks passed in preparation. A live installation with this new script has not been recorded. It leaves the instructor's cmx code alone.

docs.title: Running the Project
docs.text:
From the repository root, with Python 3.12 or newer:

make -C sports test
make -C sports history
make -C sports model
make -C sports historical-serve

The local dashboard opens at http://127.0.0.1:8000. It starts with Chicago and a 100.5-point target. The working AWS tunnel used Mac port 8001, so that dashboard opens at http://127.0.0.1:8001 while the guest server and tunnel stay open.

The historical import downloads about 18 MB into the ignored sports/data/ folder. Skip history if the historical database already exists. The fictional demo has a separate database. More commands are in the run instructions.

docs.text:

The assignment asks students to keep Jetstream usage low to preserve class hours. Use the smallest suitable VM and shelve or delete it when idle; stopping alone is not enough.
  5. Further testing: the full live AWS model panel, updated service recovery, and broader model evaluation need recorded results. More seasons and teams would help test whether the findings hold beyond this Chicago example.

Live NBA data and real player observations will be added later. Today's historical-data demo uses the completed 2014–15 season.
